data.paragraph: Health Testing — Kings & Queens
data.heading: Tested. Verified. Transparent.
data.paragraph_2: Every cat we breed is DNA tested before they are ever bred.
data.paragraph_3: We run a full Wisdom Panel Optimal Selection genetic test on every cat we breed. A cat without a completed panel does not get bred here — that is a rule, not a goal.
data.label: Health conditions screened
data.paragraph_6: Health is our promise. Transparency is our standard.
data.paragraph_21: This modifier does not cause disease on its own. Kuromi is Clear for the actual MPS VI disease variant, and breeding decisions account for both cats’ genetic results.
data.paragraph_23: See pages from Kuromi’s actual Wisdom Panel report on file.
data.paragraph_24: A gentle cheek swab is collected from each cat.
data.paragraph_25: The laboratory analyzes DNA for inherited disease variants and other genetic markers.
data.paragraph_26: No cat enters our breeding program until the completed panel is reviewed.
data.paragraph_27: Families can ask to see the full report for any breeding cat — just ask.
data.paragraph_28: DNA testing identifies inherited variants. It is not an ultrasound or echocardiogram. A genetically Clear cat can still, in principle, develop disease from a cause the test does not cover.
data.paragraph_29: Real families. Real kittens. Real care.

data.paragraph: Transparency Matters
data.heading: What These Results Mean — and What They Don't
data.paragraph_2: A DNA panel tells you what a cat inherited. It is not an ultrasound, and it is not an echocardiogram. A cat that is genetically Clear of the known PKD1 and HCM mutations can still, in principle, develop kidney or heart disease from a cause this test does not cover — that is true of every DNA-tested cat, at every cattery, anywhere.
data.paragraph_3: We would rather tell you that plainly than let a “DNA tested” badge do work it hasn't earned. What we can tell you is exactly what we tested, when we tested it, and what it found. We are glad to send you the full report for any cat on this page — just ask.

faqs.name: Do you currently have kittens available?

data.paragraph: Our availability changes frequently! Because many of our kittens are reserved during scheduled reservation periods, we may have kittens who are still growing but are not yet officially available for reservation. If we don't currently have the right kitten for you, you're welcome to join our free waitlist for upcoming litters and reservation opportunities. posts.name: Ragdoll Kittens for Washington Families: What to Check Before You Book a Trip

data.excerpt: Looking for a Ragdoll from Washington? Review the family match, parent health records and travel requirements before planning your pickup in Austin, Texas.
data.html:
If you are looking for Ragdoll kittens in Washington, you do not have to choose a breeder from one pretty photograph or a promise that sounds reassuring. You should be able to ask questions, read the records and understand how the kitten might fit into your family before you plan a trip.

Astrid Moon Cattery is our home cattery in Austin, Texas. We welcome conversations with families in Seattle, Bellevue, Redmond, Kirkland and elsewhere in Washington. We are not a Washington cattery, and we want that to be clear from the beginning. The distance is something to plan around, not something to hide.

Start With the Family Match

Tell us about the people and animals at home, your routines and the kind of companion you are hoping for. We spend time with our kittens every day, and those observations are more useful than a label such as “the cuddly boy” or “the quiet girl.” Every kitten is an individual.

Look through our current kitten profiles, photos and videos, then bring us your questions. Confirm availability directly rather than assuming that a kitten in an older post is still looking for a home. We want the kitten to become an integral part of your family, and we pay attention to the match on both sides.

Ask for the Parents’ Actual Health Records

A registry logo and the phrase “health tested” are starting points for questions, not the answers. Our currently breeding cats have genetic testing reports, and we share their reports and pedigrees on our Kings and Queens page. Young cats we are raising for the program are tested before breeding.

Genetic testing and an echocardiogram are different examinations. The UC Davis Ragdoll HCM test checks a particular HCM-associated variant; it cannot rule out every cause of heart disease. An echocardiogram is an ultrasound examination of the heart.

David Bowie, Princess (Strawberry Shortcake) and Bandit have completed echocardiograms. We are working through the remaining cats in our program. Ask which records are available for the particular parents of the kitten you are considering. A parent’s examination is not an examination of the kitten, and screening cannot promise that a cat will never develop HCM.

If you are unsure what you are looking at, our guide to reading health-testing documentation can help you prepare questions. You do not need to apologize for wanting to understand the reports.

Settle the Match Before the Itinerary

Visits to our Austin, Texas home cattery are by appointment. We can discuss pickup and whether an individually arranged in-cabin flight nanny is feasible for the placement. We do not send kittens as cargo. A flight on an airline’s timetable does not establish the kitten’s travel arrangements, the handoff or the cost.

Before booking, confirm who will accompany the kitten, where you will meet, what the quote includes and what happens if the plan changes. Read our Washington kitten-planning guidance alongside the individual kitten’s information.

A New Kitten Is Not the Same as an Established Pet Traveling With You

Washington’s official small-animal entry guidance distinguishes pets already owned for more than a month and traveling without a change of ownership from pets changing homes. Do not assume that the established-pet exemption covers bringing home a newly purchased kitten.

Have the veterinarian confirm the applicable health certificate and rabies requirements for the kitten’s age and entry date. Confirm the carrier’s requirements too. The state guidance and the actual placement need to be considered together before travel is booked.

Clear Pricing, With Travel Discussed Separately

Every companion kitten is $4,500, regardless of sex or color, with no discounts. Transportation costs are separate. Our companion kitten guide explains the included care; review the kitten’s records and current written agreement with us before reserving.

We love raising these cats and helping them find the right families. If you are considering a Ragdoll from Washington, tell us about your home or send us your questions. The conversation comes first.

State guidance checked October 27, 2026. Confirm current requirements with the veterinarian and carrier for your actual travel date and route.

posts.name: Are Ragdoll Cats Good With Dogs? A Careful Introduction Matters

data.excerpt: Our new guide starts with the dog you actually have, then covers protected cat spaces, gradual introductions, and supervision. Calm meetings and safe retreat options come first.
data.html:
Are Ragdoll Cats Good With Dogs? A Careful Introduction Matters

A Ragdoll asleep near the family dog is a lovely picture. It is the outcome many people want when they ask whether Ragdoll cats are good with dogs. The answer is that some are very comfortable with suitable dogs, but the breed name cannot tell you whether a particular pairing will be safe.

Your dog’s behavior around cats, the kitten’s experience, the household setup, and your ability to manage introductions all matter. A gentle kitten still needs protection from chasing, rough play, and overwhelming attention.

Start With the Dog You Have

Describe behavior honestly. Has your dog lived peacefully with a cat, or only watched one through a window? Can the dog notice a small moving animal and then respond to you? Does it fixate, lunge, guard food, or chase?

“Friendly” may mean friendly with adults at a park. It does not necessarily mean safe with a small kitten running across a room. A dog’s size is not a complete answer either; a small dog can frighten or injure a kitten.

If there is a history of grabbing, injuring, or intensely pursuing cats or other small animals, obtain professional behavioral guidance before bringing a kitten home. Do not use a new kitten to test whether the dog has changed.

Prepare a Cat-Only Area

Your kitten needs a room the dog cannot enter, with its own food, water, litter box, resting places, and hiding options. Plan how people will enter and leave without accidentally releasing either animal into the other’s space.

Beyond that room, think about escape routes and raised resting places the kitten can reach safely. A narrow dead end behind the sofa is not the same as a useful refuge. The kitten should not have to pass the dog to reach essential resources.

Start with our bringing-home guide, then add the arrangements your dog makes necessary.

Let Familiarity Develop Before Direct Contact

Cats Protection recommends gradual introductions, beginning with separate spaces and scent familiarity before controlled visual contact. Only progress while both animals remain comfortable.

You are looking for ordinary behavior: an animal can notice the other, disengage, and return to something else. Intense staring, repeated rushing toward the barrier, or a kitten hiding continuously are reasons to slow down, not proof that they “just need to meet.”

Keep a simple record of what each animal did. It can help you notice improvement, identify a difficult setup, and give a professional a useful description if you need help.

Make Early Meetings Easy to End

When both animals are ready for a direct supervised introduction, have enough adult help to manage them safely. Keep the dog on a lead with sufficient distance that it cannot reach the kitten. The cat should be free to retreat; do not restrain it in someone’s arms or confine it in a carrier while the dog investigates.

Reward calm behavior and keep the session brief. If the dog cannot disengage or the kitten becomes frightened, separate them calmly and return to an easier stage. Never allow chasing as part of the introduction.

The lead is a management tool, not a reason to bring the animals closer than they can handle. Distance is useful. So is ending a session while it is still going well.

Keep the Rules Consistent

  • No chasing: Do not allow it sometimes because it appears playful.
  • No forced greetings: The kitten may choose distance.
  • Separate meals: Keep food and feeding routines from becoming a point of competition.
  • Protected litter access: The cat should be able to use the box without a dog approaching.
  • Supervised shared time: Keep the animals separated whenever no adult can supervise, particularly while the cat is a kitten.

Explain these rules to children and visitors. “They seemed fine yesterday” is not a reason for someone else to remove the barrier today.

Socialization Helps, but It Does Not Transfer Automatically

Our kittens are raised in a home environment, and our website describes socialization around children, cats, and dogs. That background is useful information. It is not a guarantee that every kitten will feel comfortable with every dog in a new home.

A familiar calm dog and an unfamiliar excited dog are different experiences. Continue to protect the kitten’s ability to learn safely after go-home rather than expecting the breeder’s socialization to do all the work.

When to Reconsider the Match

Persistent fixation, repeated attempts to chase or grab, resource guarding, or a cat that cannot use the home comfortably need professional attention. Do not wait for an injury to decide that the plan is not working.

Sometimes the kindest conclusion is that a particular dog and kitten should not share a home. That is why we ask about existing pets during the application process. Please include the difficult details as well as the appealing ones.

A successful introduction is not measured by how quickly you remove a barrier. It is measured by whether both animals can live safely and comfortably in the home you are building for them.

posts.name: Introducing a Ragdoll Kitten to Another Cat: Let Comfort Set the Pace

data.excerpt: Our new introduction guide covers separate spaces, gradual steps, subtle signs of tension, and why calm coexistence matters more than an instant cuddle photo.
data.html:
Introducing a Ragdoll Kitten to Another Cat: Let Comfort Set the Pace

Your new Ragdoll kitten is coming home, and you are hoping your resident cat will be delighted. It is a lovely hope. It is also a lot to ask of a cat who did not participate in the decision.

A careful introduction gives both cats choices, space, and time. The goal at first is comfortable coexistence, not a photograph of them sleeping together. The 2024 AAFP intercat tension guidelines emphasize that tension can be subtle and that introducing a new cat is a common point at which it begins.

Ask Whether the Match Makes Sense

Before choosing a kitten, consider your resident cat’s age, activity, health, and history with other cats. A quiet senior may not appreciate being used as a playmate by a busy kitten. A cat who has struggled with other animals may need a more cautious discussion before you add one.

Tell your breeder and veterinarian what you have observed. “Friendly with people” and “comfortable sharing territory with another cat” are different things. Neither a pedigree nor an affectionate reputation guarantees compatibility.

Prepare Two Complete Living Spaces

The newcomer needs a secure transition room with food, water, litter, resting and hiding places, toys, and an appropriate scratching surface. Your resident cat should retain comfortable access to its familiar resources.

Think about routes through the home. Can one cat block the hallway that leads to the only litter box? Will a shy cat have to pass the other cat to reach water? Separate resources are useful only if each cat can reach them without pressure.

Our litter-box setup guide can help with the practical arrangement. Discuss health precautions and any separation period with your veterinarian before direct contact.

Use Stages, Not a Deadline

The AAFP guidance describes a gradual progression from separate spaces to scent familiarity, controlled visual access, and supervised proximity. Move forward when both cats are comfortable. If tension appears, step back. Some introductions take weeks or longer.

The following checkpoints help you apply that principle without turning it into a race:

  1. Settling: Is the newcomer eating, resting, exploring, and using the litter box in its own room?
  2. Familiarity: Can each cat notice the other’s scent without prolonged distress or avoidance?
  3. Seeing: Can they observe one another through a secure barrier while still choosing to move away?
  4. Sharing space: Can a short supervised session end calmly, before either cat feels trapped?

Record a few observations after each attempt. “Both cats ate afterward and returned to ordinary activity” is more informative than “we made it ten minutes.”

Look for More Than Fighting

Watch for staring, blocking access, stalking, repeated hiding, or one cat avoiding a part of the home it previously used. A household can have a problem even when no one is throwing punches.

A single hiss is information, not a moral failure. Increase distance and reconsider the situation. Do not punish a cat for communicating discomfort, and do not force it closer to prove that the other cat is harmless.

If either cat’s eating, elimination, activity, or comfort changes, involve your veterinarian. Medical discomfort and social stress can overlap; guessing at the cause can delay useful help.

Common Shortcuts That Make Things Harder

  • Opening the carrier in front of the resident cat: The newcomer immediately has an audience and limited choices. Start in the prepared room instead.
  • Holding cats nose to nose: Being restrained removes their ability to create distance.
  • Letting them “work it out”: Repeated frightening encounters can make the relationship harder to repair.
  • Rushing because the kitten seems ready: Both cats need to be comfortable, not only the more confident one.
  • Removing every familiar routine: Keep dependable attention and resources available to your resident cat.

Give Each Cat Individual Time

Your resident cat still needs the relationship it had with you before the newcomer arrived. The kitten needs its own play and attention too. Plan those periods instead of expecting the cats to entertain each other immediately.

When relatives visit, explain the introduction plan. One well-meaning person opening a door for “a quick hello” can undo the careful separation you arranged. Clear household instructions matter as much as the equipment.

What Success Can Look Like

Some cats become close companions. Others share a home comfortably while preferring separate resting places. The absence of cuddling is not, by itself, a failed introduction.

Look for both cats being able to move, eat, rest, play, and use their resources without persistent avoidance or intimidation. If progress stalls, seek a veterinarian’s guidance and, when appropriate, a qualified feline behavior professional.

Our first 48 hours guide covers the newcomer’s initial settling period. Take that foundation seriously. A kitten who has time to feel secure is in a better position to begin the next part of family life.

posts.name: Ragdoll vs. Birman: Similar Blue Eyes, Two Different Breeds

data.excerpt: Our new comparison explains markings, general build, care, and why registration matters more than identifying a cat from a photo. The artwork features Kuromi, our Ragdoll model.
data.html:
Ragdoll vs. Birman: Similar Blue Eyes, Two Different Breeds

Blue eyes, a soft coat, darker points, and white feet: a quick photograph can make a Birman and a mitted Ragdoll look remarkably similar. They are still two distinct breeds, with their own standards and histories.

If you are comparing Ragdoll vs. Birman for your next companion, start with the features the registries describe, then move to the individual cat. Appearance can narrow your questions. It should not be the only thing making the decision.

The Short Comparison

Feature Ragdoll Birman
General build A large cat of moderate type A medium-to-large, substantial cat
Eyes and coloration Blue eyes and pointed coloration Blue eyes and pointed coloration
White markings Colorpoint, mitted, and bicolor patterns differ in their white markings Distinctive white gloves and laces
Coat Semi-longhair; regular care remains important Semi-longhair; regular care remains important
Identification Registration and pedigree establish the documented breed Registration and pedigree establish the documented breed

This is a practical comparison drawn from TICA’s breed descriptions, not a method for assigning a breed to an unknown cat from its appearance.

White Feet Are a Clue, Not a Conclusion

The Birman standard describes white gloves on the feet and laces on the back of the hind legs. A mitted Ragdoll also has white feet, but its pattern is defined differently, including a white chin and belly stripe. A bicolor Ragdoll has a more extensive white pattern, including the inverted V on the face.

Those details explain why two breeds can look similar without being interchangeable. They also explain why a cat with white socks is not automatically either breed. Many wonderful cats have markings that resemble a pedigree breed without having documented ancestry.

Our Ragdoll colors and patterns guide offers a closer look at the Ragdoll side of that comparison.

Adult Size Affects Everyday Equipment

“Large cat” sounds charming until the carrier is too small or the cat tree shifts when the cat jumps onto it. Whatever breed you choose, buy equipment for the adult you expect to live with.

Ask about the parents and the breeder’s observations, while recognizing that no one can guarantee a kitten’s exact adult dimensions. Look at usable carrier space, the stability of a scratching post, and the room available to turn comfortably in a litter box.

A cat’s weight should never become a sales trophy. Comfortable movement and appropriate body condition matter more than achieving a dramatic number on a scale.

Both Breeds Still Need Grooming

A coat described as silky or relatively easy to maintain still needs attention. Find out what grooming the kitten currently accepts, which tools are used, and where the breeder checks for tangles.

Consider whether grooming fits your household in practice. Who will do it? Where will the cat feel comfortable? If someone has hand pain or limited mobility, can the setup be adapted or professional help arranged? Those are useful ownership questions regardless of breed.

Keep sessions gentle and brief, and ask for help if mats become tight or painful. Neither breed label is permission to ignore coat changes.

Temperament Comparisons Have Limits

Both breeds are often described as affectionate companions. That does not establish that every Ragdoll is calmer than every Birman, or that one breed will tolerate any amount of handling. Avoid choosing a cat on a ranking that sounds more precise than the evidence behind it.

Instead, describe your actual household: children, existing animals, work hours, activity, and what companionship means to you. “I want a cat who enjoys sitting nearby while I work” is more useful than “I want the most affectionate breed.”

Ask the breeder what they have observed repeatedly. A kitten’s choices over time tell you more than a single sleepy photograph.

Compare the Breeder as Carefully as the Breed

Once you have found a breed that appeals to you, evaluate the program behind the kitten. Review registration, the written agreement, veterinary records, the actual tests performed, and what happens before go-home.

Do not assume a registry listing is a guarantee about every business practice or future health outcome. Ask specific questions and make sure the answers connect to documents you can review.

Compare what is included rather than treating the lowest initial price as the full cost of ownership. Veterinary care, equipment, food, and backup care continue long after the purchase.

What We Offer

Astrid Moon Cattery breeds blue-eyed pointed Ragdolls only. We do not breed Birmans. Our kittens are placed in companion homes with no breeding rights, and spay/neuter is completed before go-home.

If a Ragdoll seems like the right fit, our adoption FAQ explains the process, current pricing, payment methods, and visits. Applications are reviewed before reservation; an application alone does not hold a kitten.

If a Birman ultimately suits you better, a careful comparison has done its job. The goal is to choose a companion whose needs you can meet, with accurate information about the cat and the people raising it.

posts.name: Male vs. Female Ragdoll Cats: Choose the Individual, Not the Stereotype

data.excerpt: Our new male-versus-female guide looks at size, practical care, existing pets, and the questions that help you find a good match. Both sexes can be wonderful companions.
data.html:
Male vs. Female Ragdoll Cats: Choose the Individual, Not the Stereotype

“Are the boys more cuddly?” “Are girls more independent?” These are understandable questions when you are trying to imagine life with a kitten. They are also questions that can lead you toward a confident answer the individual cat never agreed to.

For a companion Ragdoll, sex is one detail. The kitten’s behavior, experiences, comfort with handling, and fit with your household deserve much more attention. A female can be deeply affectionate. A male can prefer sitting beside you to sitting on you.

The Most Useful General Difference Is Size

Male Ragdolls are often larger than females, but individual ranges overlap. That distinction can affect equipment choices and how comfortable a person feels lifting an adult cat. It does not allow a breeder to promise an exact adult weight from a kitten photograph.

A 2025 Royal Veterinary College study of Ragdolls under UK primary veterinary care also found males heavier than females in its population. Population findings help describe a trend; they do not set a target weight for your own cat. Appropriate body condition is a veterinary question, not a competition to raise the largest Ragdoll.

If size is a practical concern, read our Ragdoll size guide. Plan the carrier, litter box, and resting spaces around an adult cat rather than the tiny kitten currently standing in front of you.

Personality Is Not a Male/Female Package

Cats Protection advises that there is little overall difference in companion personality between male and female cats, particularly after neutering. Individual background and experience matter.

That is why “boys are always sweeter” is not a useful guarantee. It may describe someone’s experience with a few cats, but it should not overrule what you can learn about the kitten you are actually considering.

Ask for observations instead of adjectives. What does the kitten do when a person sits quietly on the floor? Does it approach a new toy immediately or watch first? How does it respond when play ends? How readily does it settle after ordinary household activity?

Compare Behaviors That Matter in Your Home

Your priority A more useful question
A companion who enjoys company How does this kitten choose to spend time near people?
A quieter household What activity and noise levels does this kitten handle comfortably?
Another cat already lives here How does the kitten play, and how might that fit the resident cat?
Children in the home What supervision and handling expectations will keep everyone comfortable?
Difficulty lifting a large adult Can we plan care and equipment around realistic adult size?

None of those questions requires a kitten to perform on command during one visit. They invite a fuller conversation about repeated observations and your needs.

Our Kittens Are Placed as Companions

Astrid Moon Cattery places companion kittens with no breeding rights. Spay or neuter is completed before go-home. That means advice about managing intact breeding cats is not the right basis for comparing our companion kittens.

Spay/neuter does not turn a cat into a blank slate or guarantee the absence of every behavior problem. It is one part of responsible care. Your relationship, environment, and attention to health continue to matter throughout the cat’s life.

Our price is $4,500 per companion kitten, regardless of sex, color, pattern, or eye color. There is no “sweeter boy” surcharge or “rare girl” premium in our pricing.

What If You Already Have a Cat?

Do not reduce compatibility to “get the opposite sex.” Cats Protection states that there is no evidence that a cat necessarily prefers one sex over another. Consider the resident cat’s history, energy level, age, and willingness to share space.

A highly active kitten may be difficult for an older cat who values quiet. A shy cat may need a particularly careful introduction and several ways to avoid contact. The right answer might be a thoughtful pairing, or it might be that your current cat would be happier without another cat.

Be specific on your application. “We have a cat” tells us much less than “our ten-year-old cat has lived alone for six years and avoids visiting animals.” Details make it possible to discuss the actual situation.

Keep Preferences, but Leave Room for a Good Match

It is fine to have a preference for a male or female. You may have a familiar name in mind or a practical reason connected to size. Just leave enough room to consider a kitten whose behavior suits you well, even if that kitten is not the sex you expected to choose.

Try ranking your priorities before reviewing available kittens. Companionship, activity, handling comfort, and compatibility should have their own lines. Put appearance on the list too, but do not let a photo answer every other question for you.

What We Can Promise to Discuss

We can discuss our observations, explain our placement process, and ask honest questions about your home. We cannot promise that every male will love being carried, every female will be independent, or any kitten will behave exactly the same way in every future situation.

A good match begins with that honesty. You are choosing an individual companion for everyday life, and the everyday details are where the decision becomes meaningful.

posts.name: Can Ragdoll Cats Be Left Alone? Planning for Workdays and Real Life

data.excerpt: A settled adult and a newly arrived kitten need different plans. Our new guide helps you think through meals, company, safe activity, and backup care before choosing a companion.
data.html:
Can Ragdoll Cats Be Left Alone? Planning for Workdays and Real Life

You can have a job and be a thoughtful cat owner. The useful question is not whether you ever leave home. It is whether the particular cat’s feeding, supervision, health, and social needs will be met while you are away.

Some adult Ragdolls manage an ordinary workday with a suitable routine. A newly arrived kitten needs a different plan. There is no single safe number of hours that applies to every cat simply because the registration says Ragdoll.

Separate the Workday From the Weekend Away

A familiar adult cat spending part of the day at home is one situation. A young kitten spending its first week in an unfamiliar house is another. Leaving any cat for a weekend with an overflowing bowl and an automatic feeder is a third, and it should not be treated as an extended version of the first.

Cats Protection advises much more frequent checks for young kittens and for cats with medical or other complex needs. Its general time limits are not a personal recommendation for your kitten. Plan around the cat’s age, feeding schedule, care instructions, and actual response to being alone.

Before Adoption, Map an Ordinary Tuesday

Write down when you leave, when someone can visit, and when you reliably return. Include commuting, school pickup, recurring appointments, and the evening when work usually runs late. A schedule that works only on your shortest day needs a backup.

Then assign the care: who provides meals, refreshes water, checks the litter box, and spends time with the cat? “Someone will probably be home” is less useful than naming the person and confirming that they have agreed.

If your days are consistently long, consider whether an adult cat whose habits are already understood would fit better than a young kitten. Our retired Ragdoll adoption guide explains that separate possibility when a suitable adult is available. It is not a promise of current availability.

Give a New Kitten Time to Settle

Try to arrange go-home around a period when you can be present and observe the transition. That does not mean holding the kitten constantly. It means noticing whether it is eating, drinking, resting, and using the litter box, and responding when something needs attention.

Practice brief departures after the kitten is comfortable in its safe room. Return calmly and observe what happened. Build gradually rather than introducing a full workday as the first separation. Our first 48 hours guide covers the settling-in period in more detail.

If your work cannot flex, arrange reliable help before pickup. A rushed solution after the kitten arrives places the pressure on everyone, including the kitten.

What a Workday Setup Needs

  • Reliable care: Meals and checks suited to the cat, with a named person available when needed.
  • A safe indoor space: Secure doors and windows, comfortable resting options, and access to water and litter.
  • Appropriate activity: Safe toys your cat can use without supervision; put away string and wand toys after shared play.
  • Predictable attention: Time together before and after work that fits the cat’s preferences.
  • A backup: Someone who can enter the home if transport, illness, or an emergency delays you.

Technology can support this plan. It cannot become the whole plan. A camera may show you a tipped water bowl, but a person still has to refill it. An automatic feeder does not assess whether a cat is refusing food or feeling unwell.

For practical ideas on resting places, vertical space, and keeping resources separate, see our guide to creating a Ragdoll-friendly apartment. Those principles are useful in a larger home, too.

Would a Second Cat Solve the Problem?

Possibly a well-matched companion could enrich a cat’s life, but another cat is not a guaranteed remedy for loneliness. Cats Protection notes that temperament and compatibility matter more than a simple male/female pairing rule. Some cats enjoy feline company; others find sharing their space difficult.

Two kittens also still need feeding, observation, veterinary care, and a safe environment. Buying a second cat does not remove the need for a person to show up.

Describe your household honestly when discussing a match. The best answer may be one cat, a compatible pair, an adult, a different timing, or waiting until your schedule changes.

If you decide a second cat is a good fit, our guide to introducing a Ragdoll kitten to another cat explains how to let their comfort set the pace.

Watch the Individual, Not an Internet Stereotype

Do not assume that a quiet cat is content or that a cat greeting you enthusiastically has been distressed all day. Look for patterns in eating, play, litter use, rest, and interaction.

If you notice persistent changes, record when they happen and contact your veterinarian. Avoid labeling house-soiling, reduced appetite, or overgrooming as “separation anxiety” without considering a medical explanation. A short video or simple written log can help you describe the concern more clearly.

A Sustainable Plan Is Better Than a Perfect-Sounding Promise

You do not have to promise never to leave the house. You do need a plan that still works when a meeting runs late or your regular helper is unavailable. Ask yourself whether you can afford that backup care and whether you will actually use it.

At Astrid Moon Cattery, our application asks about your home because the match matters. Tell us the real schedule. It is much easier to discuss practical arrangements before a kitten is reserved than to discover afterward that everyone’s assumptions were different.

posts.name: Do Ragdoll Cats Shed? A Grooming Routine That Fits Real Life

data.excerpt: Our new guide covers gentle combing, useful tools, checking for tangles, and coat changes that deserve veterinary attention. Start with the individual cat and build a routine you can keep.
data.html:
Do Ragdoll Cats Shed? A Grooming Routine That Fits Real Life

Yes, Ragdoll cats shed. If you are picturing a beautiful, fluffy companion whose coat somehow never appears on your sofa, I would rather reset that expectation before you bring a kitten home.

A manageable grooming routine is a much more useful promise than a “non-shedding” cat. The goal is to keep the coat comfortable, notice changes, and make handling familiar. You should not have to turn every combing session into a wrestling match.

Start With the Coat in Front of You

Two Ragdolls in the same home may not need exactly the same amount of grooming. Coat length, texture, age, season, and the cat’s ability to groom itself can affect the work involved. A kitten’s coat also will not necessarily tell you what its adult routine will look like.

Begin with frequent, brief checks. Look and feel gently behind the ears, under the front legs, along the sides, and around the back legs. You are learning where this particular cat develops tangles, not completing a universal number of brush strokes.

A small amount of loose hair on your hand is a different issue from a bald patch, irritated skin, or a sudden change in grooming. Keep that distinction in mind before buying another tool.

A Useful Comb Beats a Drawer Full of Gadgets

The Feline Veterinary Medical Association’s Cat Friendly Homes guidance describes a comb with long, rounded teeth as a useful starting tool. A brush can smooth the surface while leaving a tangle underneath, so check gently through the coat rather than judging only by how tidy the top looks.

Let your cat inspect the tool. Touch an easy area briefly, then stop and reward calm participation. If the comb catches, do not pull harder. Investigate what is catching and whether you need professional help.

Store grooming supplies where you will actually use them. A comb beside the chair where your cat likes attention may be more useful than an elaborate kit in a cupboard you rarely open.

Build a Routine You Can Repeat

Here is a practical starting framework, not a fixed veterinary prescription:

  • Daily check: During ordinary petting, notice loose hair, small knots, sore areas, and whether your cat is comfortable being touched.
  • Short combing sessions: Work on one manageable area, take breaks, and gradually cover the coat. Increase frequency if tangles are beginning to form.
  • Weekly household reset: Wash suitable bedding according to its care label, clean grooming tools, and remove shed fur from favorite resting places.
  • Reassess: If the routine leaves knots behind, adjust it. If your cat becomes distressed, shorten the sessions and ask for help with technique.

RSPCA guidance emphasizes regular, short grooming sessions and notes that some longhaired cats need daily attention. Your cat’s comfort and coat condition matter more than a claim that all Ragdolls need exactly the same schedule.

What to Do About a Mat

A tight mat is not simply extra fluff. Pulling at it can hurt, and skin can lie surprisingly close beneath it. Do not cut into mats with scissors. Dense, painful, or skin-adjacent mats are a reason to contact a veterinarian or an experienced cat groomer.

You do not need to finish the whole coat in one sitting. If your cat tenses, moves away repeatedly, growls, or begins sharply swishing its tail, pause. A cooperative five minutes is more useful than a long session that makes the next one harder.

When asking for professional help, explain where the mats are, how long they have been present, and whether touching the area seems painful. That gives the person helping you a clearer starting point.

Shedding and Allergies Are Different Questions

Removing loose coat can make your home easier to clean, but it does not make a Ragdoll hypoallergenic. If someone in your household has cat allergies, read our separate Ragdoll allergy guide and discuss the person’s needs with their clinician before making a commitment.

Do not choose a kitten on the assumption that one sex, color, or particularly silky coat will solve allergies. A grooming plan addresses coat care; it cannot guarantee a person’s medical response.

Make the Home Easier to Maintain

Choose a few resting spots with washable covers, keep a lint roller where you get dressed, and use a cleaning routine you can sustain. Our apartment setup guide can help you plan those resting areas alongside litter access, play and safe retreat spaces. You can love a longhaired cat and still prefer not to wear its coat to every appointment.

Try changing one part of the routine at a time. If you replace the brush, shampoo, food, and cleaning products together, it becomes harder to work out which change helped or irritated your cat. Diet changes belong in a thoughtful care plan, not a desperate response to finding hair on a cushion.

When a Coat Change Needs a Vet

Seek veterinary advice about excessive licking, bald areas, damaged skin, a newly greasy or unkempt coat, or a cat that suddenly stops tolerating grooming. Cat Friendly Homes notes that changes in self-grooming can accompany discomfort or illness. Grooming should help you notice those changes, not cover them up.

A Ragdoll’s coat is part of the daily responsibility of living with one. If short, regular care fits your life, that beautiful coat can be very manageable. If it does not, it is kinder to recognize the mismatch before choosing a kitten.

BEP Ragdolls vs. Cherubim: What the Names Mean Before You Buy

You start looking for a Ragdoll kitten, and suddenly the names multiply. Traditional Ragdoll. BEP. Mink. Sepia. Cherubim. Some listings use several of those words together, which makes an ordinary question surprisingly difficult: what breed am I actually being offered?

BEP means blue-eyed pointed. It describes the Ragdoll’s blue eyes and pointed coloration. In TICA’s current breed group, Ragdoll uses the code RD; Cherubim uses CB and has a different set of accepted color categories. Astrid Moon Cattery breeds BEP Ragdolls only. We do not breed Cherubim.

That is a clear description of our program, not a judgment about another family’s cat. Buyers deserve accurate names and paperwork, and every cat deserves thoughtful care.

What Does Blue-Eyed Pointed Mean?

On a pointed cat, the face, ears, legs, and tail carry deeper color than the body. White markings may overlay that pattern. A bicolor Ragdoll’s white face and legs do not make the cat non-pointed, and a mitted Ragdoll is still pointed underneath the white markings.

BEP is not a separate breed called the “BEP Ragdoll.” It is useful shorthand for the combination described in the Ragdoll standard. It also is not a health certificate, a temperament test, or proof of a particular ancestry. Those are separate questions with separate documentation.

How TICA Distinguishes Ragdoll and Cherubim

TICA’s Ragdoll Breed Group standard, updated May 1, 2025, distinguishes the two breeds as follows. These are TICA categories; do not assume every registry uses identical registration rules.

Question Ragdoll (RD) Cherubim (CB)
Color category Pointed Mink, sepia, and traditional color categories
Eyes Blue Accepted colors depend on the color category
Body type Large, semi-longhaired cat of moderate type Shares the breed group’s general body and head type
Our program We breed BEP Ragdolls We do not breed Cherubim

The official Cherubim breed page and the current TICA standards are better reference points than an advertisement using “rare” as its explanation.

“Traditional” Is a Particularly Confusing Word

People use “traditional” in more than one way. A breeder may use it informally for the familiar blue-eyed pointed appearance. A pedigree discussion may use “traditional lines” for a particular ancestry definition. TICA also uses Traditional as a formal color-category term in the Cherubim standard.

Those uses are not interchangeable. A word on a sales page does not tell you which definition the seller intends. Ask them to explain it in plain language and show how the description connects to the cat’s registration.

For the same reason, BEP appearance alone does not establish a foundation-only pedigree. If ancestry is important to your decision, investigate the pedigree itself. Our pedigree guide addresses the separate task of reading ancestry information.

What About Listings That Say “Mink Ragdoll”?

You will still encounter older terminology, older registration documents, and marketing language that has not caught up with current standards. A listing may be outdated, imprecise, or describing registration under another system. You cannot tell which simply by reading two words.

Ask what registry issued the paperwork, what breed and color are recorded, and whether the seller’s description reflects the rules that apply to that cat. If the answers remain unclear, contact the registry using the contact information on its own website. You do not need to accept a confusing explanation because a kitten is beautiful.

A Photo Can Show Markings. It Cannot Replace a Pedigree.

Lighting, editing, age, and the camera can all affect how a coat looks online. A photograph is useful for seeing an individual cat, but it is not a complete registration record. Blue eyes alone do not prove that a cat is a Ragdoll, either.

Keep the questions separate: What does this cat look like? What does its registration say? What health records are available? What has the breeder observed about its behavior? A strong buying decision considers all four.

Five Questions to Ask Before Reserving a Kitten

  1. What breed name and registry will appear on my kitten’s paperwork?
  2. Which color and pattern are recorded, and what do those terms mean?
  3. Can you explain the parents’ registration and provide the relevant pedigree information?
  4. Which actual health reports can I review, and what are the limits of those tests?
  5. What does the written agreement say about companion placement, payment, and the health guarantee?

Ask those questions before payment. A clear answer should not require you to become a genetics expert or memorize every color code.

What We Breed at Astrid Moon Cattery

Our focus is blue-eyed pointed Ragdolls for companion homes, with no breeding rights. Our kittens are spayed or neutered before going home. We discuss the individual kitten and your household rather than treating a color label as a promise about personality.

The current written terms explain payment details. Breed terminology should help you understand what you are choosing, while the agreement explains what you are committing to.
